Furthermore, Nadal holds a dominating 13-7 head-to-head record over Federer, including victory in the epic 2008 Wimbledon final and the 2009 Australian Open final. For some purists, it is difficult to crown a player as the undisputed greatest of all time when he holds a losing record against his chief contemporary rival.

Historians also point to Rod Laver, who won the Calendar Year Grand Slam twice (in 1962 and 1969), a feat Federer has come tantalizingly close to achieving but has never completed. Meanwhile, Pete Sampras accumulated his 14 titles in an era dominated by serve-and-volley specialists, playing on radically different surfaces than today's homogenized courts.

### A Legacy Beyond Debate?

When asked directly if he now considers himself the greatest, Federer remained characteristically modest. 

"It’s hard to say," Federer replied. "I'm proud of my career, for sure. I've achieved much more than I ever thought I would. But tennis is a sport where every generation brings new champions. Rod Laver, Pete Sampras... they are legends."

Whether or not the consensus is unanimous, the 2009 French Open feels like a watershed moment. At just 27 years old, Federer has tied Sampras's record in significantly less time—and with Wimbledon just three weeks away, he is the heavy favorite to win a 15th title and break the record outright on the lush grass of the All England Club.

For years, the tennis world debated whether Federer *could* stand alone as the greatest ever. On Sunday in Paris, he removed the final barrier standing in his way. The debate may linger in barbershops and commentary booths, but on the courts, Roger Federer’s legend is now complete.
